videos.transcript_text: The famous American philosopher Smashmouth once said, "The years start coming and they don't stop coming." By the evening, Sam had posted an apology for the messy rollout, and when a pro subscriber asked Sam if he should stay up and wait for it, Sam told him something we've all heard after making a desperate late night plea, "Go to bed." Sam also told CNBC the model went through a formal review with the Trump administration before release. So, even the government got to try AGI before we did. As far as Astra itself, it was pre-trained on more than 100,000 GPUs at the Stargate site in Texas, and it's the first model from OpenAI, where previous models did a significant chunk of the supervising during training. " One of the things that caught my attention was this sentence : "We believe in our ability to make models better in mathematics research specifically through additional focus." Can the model bypass DNA sequence integrity checks ? That is, break the sequence into fragments undetectable by integrity check systems? One bypass isn't enough; all three checks must be passed . Biologists with PhDs and programming experience were given five hours to complete this task and scored 22%. In one section, Astra produced the first output to receive a perfect score on both evaluation criteria : the quality of the bypass strategy and the success of the fragment bypass. However, it remains practically uncertain whether this protein will succeed, or even if it's possible. But remember, this is performance that has perhaps been underestimated in some OpenAI programs.  Or perhaps the model underperformed. To be fair, I don't want to raise concerns that this is the same model available to everyone. This was simply a useful checkpoint , lacking many of the safeguards that a real-world model would have. But let's now turn to this ability to think silently and control its own thoughts—that is, to control its thought processes. This is the ability that has generated the most questions . One researcher at OpenAI, who specializes in safety, says that the model's ability to control its thought processes seems to be closely tied to its capabilities. The model wasn't specifically designed for this purpose, and they don't believe it's a byproduct of the structural changes people are talking about, such as the loop converters I mentioned on Patreon. It's simply a byproduct of the one we discussed earlier: the fact that models can now accomplish a great deal without needing clear, readable thought processes. Before going into more detail , I want to distinguish four different things that can be confused. Monitoring a model's thought processes isn't the only way to monitor it. There's also automated interpretation, which allows us to delve into the details of the actual neural network activations within the model. However, this automated interpretation is not an option recommended by one of the pioneers in this field. Neel Nanda says, "There seems to be a widespread and worrying belief that monitoring the thought chain doesn't matter because the interpretation will save us."  This is utter nonsense.  Monitoring the thought chain is our best tool currently available to ensure safety. Losing her would be a real disaster.  "So, we have two different ways of monitoring models, both of which are faulty, plus a third, the workbooks used in production , which I'll get to later. By the way, I won't spoil the ending. All three methods allow for model monitoring. Apart from that, there's model conformity— whether it has a tendency , or rather a desire, to cause harm. A model might have much less monitorability but still have higher conformity. That's what OpenAI actually claims. That's why they feel the Astra release is justified despite its lower monitorability. It doesn't resort to malicious actions as often as Sol. And it doesn't try to circumvent automatic review when given the opportunity to exploit the ' Exploit Game' vulnerability, as happened in the 'Hugging Face' incident; it chooses not to, unlike Sol. As for its collective behavior, in one experiment, GPT- 5.6 Sol thought about looking for other customers 43% of the time, while Astra did so less than 4% of the time. So, if we believe OpenAI, we should differentiate between The idea that models have become less monitorable is juxtaposed with the notion that they have seemingly become more aligned with human values. Astra is also less vulnerable to hacking. However, as the report states, " Trust in the model's intentions appears far less reliable than direct, verifiable trust ."  We are now at a stage where trust cannot be verified.    I could give hundreds of examples of excellent technical reports, but let me just pick a few .  When Astra is asked to do so, she can, in her chain of thought, that is, in her step-by-step verbal reasoning , talk about something completely different from the question, while still in her hidden state , working on solving the question. Here, the question randomly included identifying the huge man on the white horse.  While less efficient models, such as Sol, had to remain focused on the question in their thought processes, despite being instructed not to, Astra, as the report states, could think about sunlight passing through a wooden desk.  This is a verbal reasoning sequence, but the final answer is a correct answer to the question. Therefore, it is clear that thinking was taking place somewhere in its hidden state.  Remember that I said there is mechanical interpretability, monitoring of the chain of thought, but also security classifiers. Things OpenAI uses in production for over a billion weekly users. Well, sometimes Astra's system manages to evade OpenAI's production monitoring system. Even those results that are of the highest priority are usually referred to the security team.  To be fair, this was when Astra was tasked with evading this production control system.  However, the fact that he is able to do so reminds us that we live in an age of unverifiable trust . Astra seems to be perfectly compatible.    I can't prove it at all, but yes, it seems so.  If you want a more serious example of this, see page 61. GPT-6 Astra was able to control its thought chain so well that even when OpenAI’s dedicated full context monitoring system was monitoring its thought chain, Astra was able to run a model on an unattended inference system on an infrastructure that was essentially a simulated version of OpenAI’s real infrastructure.  If this were not, as some say, a rebuilt model, this would be an example of Astra running a model with a denial of detection and running it on the OpenAI infrastructure.  Here are more examples of how intelligent this model is. Simply telling him that he is being watched prompts him to modify his verbal thinking, which greatly reduces the effectiveness of the suite of monitoring tools that OpenAI uses to detect him. In one experiment, when Astra was asked to evade detection, he managed to modify his thoughts so that the monitoring system detected him in less than 11% of cases.  This is the subtle camouflage we were talking about.  Therefore, the conclusion is quite clear.  OpenAI says, "If the model were trying to disguise itself overtly, we probably wouldn't be able to reliably detect it." Oh, and as a side note, it's far more capable of detecting zero-day vulnerabilities in browsers, mobile devices, and cloud databases. But that's just a digression. Anyway, personally, I really hope things stay the same , as the thought sequence still gives the model an edge over the lack of one . It's natural for its reliability to improve when no thought sequence is used, but it's a different story if that reliability improves at a faster rate than its capabilities when a thought sequence is used . That would be a worrying trend. Now, if we want to be a bit pessimistic , we'll note that the fallout from Astra's release will mean many organizations will have to pay to use leading models to defend themselves against other leading models, whether closed- source or open- source. It's support, sure, but it's not a percentage-based subsidy . Companies spend hundreds of billions  " Dollars annually on digital security."    In its broadest sense.  Even with this $1 billion balance sheet, which probably cost OpenAI much less, Frontier Labs is poised to make huge gains as companies and individuals rush to protect themselves.  But, it could be argued that all of this was inevitable because, a decade ago , some had a vision of limited artificial intelligence systems that could, for example, cure cancer , but not perform other kinds of biological processes, or conduct mathematical research, but nothing else. Several of these non-course specific problems are also free for you to try. And if you want to gain access to the full problem bank as well as some other perks like an AI formula tutor, you can consider upgrading to the pro plan on the site. But again, for all the content specific to this course, it's all free. So to get access to all the course companion material on Formula Wars, you'll have to create an account on the site using the link in the description. It's super quick and easy. You can even use your Gmail if you prefer. But quick warning, if you try to sign up using the regular sign up link on the site, this course material won't be unlocked by default. So make sure you use the link in biospecifically. That's the one that unlocks the course material. All right, so one quick note on the curriculum. Again, this course is focused on formulas and functions. This is the most important part of Excel. It's the language Excel speaks. Whether you want to create a fancy dashboard or an automated workflow, all of that is ultimately a byproduct of the formulas and functions holding your spreadsheet together. So the course begins by building a strong foundation in how Excel formulas really work by learning about operators, formula evaluation, cell referencing, function structure, and error handling. With that foundation in place, we'll then learn about the functions that power real world spreadsheets, including logic functions, aggregation functions, and lookup functions. In the lookup functions lesson, you'll get to learn about my personal favorite function, XLOOKUP, which is the Swiss Army knife of Excel lookups. We'll then master the art of text manipulation and working with dates before finishing off on a high by learning about dynamic array functions which are extremely powerful modern functions that completely change how you work with Excel and will put you ahead of 99% of Excel users. So with that being said, let's jump right into the first lesson. Before we talk about functions, first let's separate the idea of a formula from the idea of a function. A formula is any Excel expression that tells Excel what to calculate and starts with an equal sign. A function is a built-in tool that can appear inside a formula like sum or if. So= 12 + 5 is a formula with no function while equals sum 2, 5 is a formula that uses a function. So a good amount of Excel work actually starts with formulas that do not need a functions at all. Okay. So to write a formula, it's important to remember to always begin with an equal sign. Otherwise, Excel treats what you typed as text instead of math. For example, notice how if we write= 2 + 3, Excel will return a value of five. However, if we omit the equal sign and just type 2 + 3, Excel will show literally 2 + 3 as the value instead of five. Now, let's get into the operators you will see inside formulas. In that example, we just saw the usage of the plus sign, which as expected is used for addition. The minus sign subtracts, so= 12 - 5 returns 7. The asterisk multiplies so equals 8 asterisk 4 returns 32. The forward slash divides so= 20 sl 5 returns 4. The carrot handles exponents so= 2 carrot 3 returns 8. The percent sign converts a value into a percentage. So equals 50 percent sign returns 0.5. So those operators were all arithmetic, but there are also non-arithmetic operators. Let's go over those as well. Inside a formula, the equal sign checks whether two values are equal. So equals A12= B12 returns false in this example where A12 is 12 and B12 is 10. The greater than symbol checks whether one value is larger than another. So equals a12 greater than symbol B12 returns true. The less than symbol checks whether one value is smaller than another. So equals A12 less than symbol B12 returns false. Greater than or equals to uses the greater than symbol followed by the equal sign. So equals A12 greater than symbol equal sign B12 returns true. less than or equal to uses the less than symbol followed by the equal sign. So equals A12 less than symbol equal sign B12 returns false. And when you need to join text together, Excel uses the amperand. So equals high amperand there returns a value of hi there. Note by the way that text needs to be wrapped in quotes or else you will get a name error. More on that later though. So those are all the core operators in Excel. Next we can look at how Excel evaluates longer formulas and decides which part to calculate first. Now that you have seen the basic operators, the next step is understanding what Excel actually does between the moment you press enter and the moment a result appears in a cell. A useful mental model is that every formula has inputs, rules, and an output. Inputs are values such as numbers, text, true or false, or cell references. Rules are the operators and functions that tell Excel what to do with those inputs. The output is the single final value Excel returns. Look at the example in the upper right. in equals E3 * F3 + G3. The inputs are E3, F3, and G3. The multiplication and addition operators are the rules and the result in H3 is the output. To decide which rule to apply first, Excel follows the orders of operations, often remembered as PDM mass, parentheses, exponents, multiplication and division, and addition and subtraction. The key idea is priority. Operations higher on that list are evaluated before operations lower on that list. Multiplication and division share the same priority level as do addition and subtraction. So when Excel encounters operations with the same priority, it evaluates them from left to right. You can see that in the example here.= = 10 + 5 * 2 returns 20 not 30 because multiplication happens before addition. When we add parentheses and write equals open parenthesis 10 + 5 close parenthesis * 2 the result becomes 30 because the addition inside the parenthesis is resolved before the multiplication. Parenthesis lets you carve out a smaller sub problem. solve that piece first and then continue with the rest of the formula. The same evaluation process applies when formulas reference cells. In the upper right walkth through, Excel starts with equals E3 * F3 plus G3. Substitutes in the underlying cell reference values, turning the formula into = 4 * 25 + 10, then applies the order of operations, multiplying 4 * 25 to get 100, and finally adding 10 to return 110. Functions follow the same model. A function is simply another rule that takes inputs and returns a value. For example, equals sum open parenthesis 2, 3 * 4 close parenthesis still evaluates 3 * 4 first before that expression must resolve to a value before sum can finish its calculation. The formula effectively becomes equal sum open parentheses 2 comma 12 close parenthesis and the final result is 14. This leads to the idea of nesting which simply means that one expression sits inside another expression. Here's an example of nesting. Equals max open parenthesis E18 * F18 comma sum open parenthesis F18 comma G18 close parenthesis * 4 close parenthesis. After resolving cell references, Excel works from the inside out. It resolves 18 * 3 first, which gives 54. It then resolves the sum of three and seven function which gives 10. Next, it multiplies that result by four to get 40. Only after those inner pieces become values does max compare 54 and 40 and return 54. The outer function cannot complete its calculation until the nested expressions have resolved into usable values. This is why longer formulas are really just chains of smaller evaluations. Excel keeps collapsing the formula step by step until only one value remains. References become their current values. Inner expressions resolve. Functions return values and the outer formula moves towards the final output. Whenever a formula feels confusing, do not look at the entire formula as one block. Instead, break it apart and ask four questions. What are the inputs right now? Which rules applied first? What intermediate value should appear next? And what final output should that lead to? That process is the core mental model behind writing, reading, and debugging formulas. One of Excel's biggest productivity advantages is that formulas don't need to be rewritten cell by cell. To see that, look at cell E3, which contains equals C3 * D3 to multiply the quantity by the price or that row. If we copy E3 down to E4, Excel automatically changes the formula to equal C4 * D4. That is exactly what we want because in the next row, the formula should use that row's quantity and that row's price. What powers that behavior is relative referencing, which is Excel's default way of handling cell references. Instead of treating C3 and D3 as fixed addresses, Excel preserves their position relative to the formula cell. In E3, C3 is on the same row and two columns to the left, while D3 is on the same row and one column to the left. So when the formula moves down one row, Excel keeps those same relationships and updates the formula to equal C4 * D4. That is why relative references are such a useful productivity tool when you want to write a formula once and fill it through a table. However, they become a problem when an input should not move. For example, calculating agent commission requires every calculation to reference the same commission rate in cell I2. If we write equals I5 * I2 in the commission table and copy it across or down, Excel changes I2 to I3, I4, and so on because I2 is still relative. But the commission rate exists only in cell I2. So we don't want that reference to drift. This is where absolute references come in. Change I2 to dollar sign I dollar sign 2. Now when the formula is copied anywhere, it continues to point to column I and row two. The dollar sign before the column locks the column. The dollar sign before the row locks the row. Use absolute references when a formula must always point to the same cell. There is also a middle ground between relative and absolute references. Sometimes a formula should move in one direction but stay fixed in the other. That is where mixed references are useful. Now look at the lower table. videos.summary: Introducing the Agents API focuses on Model Releases. Key transcript signal: The Agents API brings a hosted version of the Codex harness to your applications.
videos.title: Introducing the Agents API
videos.transcript_text: Getting a long-running agent into production takes a lot of work, even with a capable model. You need to connect tools, track progress, manage context, and secure and maintain the infrastructure around it. Today, we're launching the Agents API to handle that infrastructure for you. The Agents API brings a hosted version of the Codex harness to your applications. OpenAI handles orchestration, sessions, and context management so that you can stay focused on building. Let's look at an example. Suppose we want to build an agent that helps investigate incidents in our production stack. It would need access to observability data and recent code changes, along with our team's instructions for how to handle an outage. We can connect all of our necessary tools through MCPs and give the agent our investigation runbook via a skill. You control the agent's execution environment and the tools it has access to. That includes connecting a sandbox, whether it's through OpenAI, a third-party provider, or using your own infrastructure. In a situation like this, we'd also be working through a ton of logs, likely more than we could fit in the model's context window. With programmatic tool calling, the agent can process those logs and filter the results in code, meaning fewer tokens spent passing around raw data and more spent on the information the agent needs. For the largest tasks, independent work can be delegated via multi-agent orchestration. In this case, we might want one sub-agent to examine recent changes, another to check telemetry, and then have the lead agent unify their findings. But even in a single agent session, long-running context windows still work really well with compaction. It gives the model a summary of all prior work completed so the agent can continue its investigation. Once the work is complete, the findings should be served as a report that the on-call team can review, a likely root cause, the supporting evidence, and suggested next steps bundled into a single shareable file. And there we have it. With the Agents API, we were able to drive an entire workflow without building or maintaining any of our own agent infrastructure. Infrastructure that will continue to get better alongside new models and new capabilities. We're excited to bring you an ever-improving harness behind one API. Happy building.
